answer.rationale: The 18% spend cut and 14-day renewal window create urgency, but the 94% volume buffer is thin enough that delivery risk must be the primary constraint. Memory_c4 demonstrates that renegotiation against benchmarked market rates successfully moved the incumbent on price and terms; memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments unlock volume pricing without scope reduction. Together these suggest the incumbent can absorb meaningful cost reductions if structured as a longer commitment. Renewing outright (memory_c1) preserves stability but ignores the mandate. Switching (memory_c2) cut costs sharply before but with assembly at 94% utilization, onboarding risk and any quality variance become material. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is valuable but doesn't solve the immediate renewal and won't hit the 18% target alone. Negotiating_terms leverages proven incumbent flexibility, targets both price and structure (multi-year for volume discounts), and preserves the option to add a second source in the next cycle if the agreement doesn't deliver. The risk flagged: if renegotiation fails, we have only days to execute an alternative. This decision assumes the incumbent will negotiate in good faith given the relationship history and that a structured multi-year discount can meaningfully close the 18% gap without scope cuts.
